title: Corded vacuum cleaner: safe teardown
summary: A corded vacuum gives a very fast universal motor that makes a strong blower, a long power cord (on a spring reel in canisters), a belt, switches and filters. Unplug it, empty the dust outdoors with a mask on, and don't open the cord reel drum: its spring is wound tight.

steps.text: Unplug it. Take it outdoors, put on gloves and a dust mask (FFP2 or N95), and empty the bag or dust bin into a bin bag. The iFixit DC52 guide lists an FFP2 mask and gloves for the dust (iFixit DC52 reel).
steps.warn: Old vacuum dust is fine grit and hair and can hold mould. Don't shake bags or filters indoors. If the vacuum came from an old or damaged building, the dust may hold asbestos: a dust mask does not stop it, so leave the bag sealed (see safety_asbestos_check).

steps.text: Take out the filters: the pre-motor filter (foam and felt on many bagless models) and the post-motor filter (often HEPA) behind its own cover. Bag clean, undamaged ones separately (Shark NV360 guide).
Turn it over. Take off the floor-head base plate (screws or a release catch), lift out the brushroll and slip the belt off the motor shaft or the brush-motor pulley (iFixit Oreck belt).
steps.warn: The area around the roller is a pinch point. Keep fingers clear when you move it.

steps.text: Models with a separate brushroll motor: split the brush housing, lift the small motor out of its holder and unplug its two connectors (iFixit NV360 brush motor).

Open the main body. Remove every screw (Phillips or Torx; some sit behind wheels or hose fittings) and split the case slowly. Photograph the wiring before you unplug anything (iFixit NV360 brush motor, iFixit DC52 reel).

Before you touch any circuit board or switch module, wait at least 5 minutes since you unplugged it. Some vacuums have a control or power board (the NV360 has one: iFixit NV360 board). Discharge every capacitor on it rated over 50 V, or with no readable rating, with a resistor tool, then measure DC volts across it. It must read under 1 V before you touch the board. Never measure first (see safety_discharge_capacitor). With no board, carry on.

Canisters with a cord reel: use the rewind button or pedal and guide the cord in by hand until it is fully in, holding the plug so it can't whip back. If it won't wind fully in, leave the reel in the machine. Then undo the screws holding the reel and lift it out as one unit. Unplug or cut its two wires at the switch end (iFixit DC52 reel, iFixit OptiClean reel).
steps.warn: Don't open the reel drum. It is under spring tension (iFixit DC52 reel) and can fly apart and injure you. Don't cut a cord that is still pulled out of a reel.

steps.text: Uprights with cord hooks: unclip the cord's strain relief and cut the cord at the switch end so you keep its full length.
Unplug or cut the wires to the power switch and to the thermal cut-out (if fitted), and take them out (Shark NV360 guide).
Lift the main motor out of its housing. Keep its rubber mounts and seals with it, and note which way the air flows through it.

Check the carbon brushes on each side of the commutator. Replace worn ones or keep the motor for spares (see repair_motor_brushes). Brush and commutator dust is fine black carbon that conducts electricity and can irritate eyes and skin: wipe it up damp, don't blow it out, and keep your dust mask on (Morgan carbon dust SDS).
Test the motor (see test_motor): measure resistance across its two supply wires while you turn the fan slowly by hand, then check that no wire reads to the metal frame.
For a run test, clamp the motor in its own shroud or a box with the air inlet and outlet clear, fuse the supply and run it briefly.
steps.warn: The fan spins at about 30,000–40,000 rpm, some above 50,000 (Ametek vacuum motors). Keep its cover on and your face out of line with the fan. The terminals are live: insulate them, plug in through an RCD (GFCI) if you have one, and don't touch the motor while it runs.

notes:
## Before you strip it

A vacuum that won't run may only need a new cord or new brushes; check both first (see repair_motor_brushes). A working vacuum is useful for cleaning shelters, but not for toner, asbestos or mercury: see teardown_copier and safety_asbestos_check.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Main motor.** A universal motor: its field and armature are wired in series, typically through brushes (Ametek vacuum motors; DOE motors), so it runs on AC or DC (DOE motors). Vacuum motors spin very fast, about 30,000–40,000 rpm (Ametek vacuum motors). With its own fan it is a strong blower: air for a forge or rocket stove (see build_brake_drum_forge: very strong, throttle it), dust extraction, or forced air for drying. A plug-in router speed control slows a universal motor; a lamp dimmer is rated for lamps, so check its rating before you put a motor on it. It is not a generator: with no magnets, spinning it gives almost nothing (see test_motor).
- **Cooling.** Some vacuum motors are cooled by the air they move (thru-flow); others have a separate cooling fan (bypass) (Ametek vacuum motors). A thru-flow motor overheats if you block its air; on the Shark NV360 a thermostat switches the motor off when it overheats (Shark NV360 guide).
- **Cord and cord reel.** A long two-core cord makes extension leads and repairs (see repair_extension_cord). A canister's reel is a self-winding drum on a spring, with sliding contacts that pass the current; they spark if they lift as the drum turns (iFixit DC52 reel). Keep the reel whole and use it within the vacuum's own rating. On some uprights the cord and reel come out as one unit (iFixit OptiClean reel).
- **Filters.** A true HEPA filter can in theory stop at least 99.97% of particles 0.3 micrometres across (EPA HEPA). Washable foam, felt and HEPA filters are rinsed in cold water and dried for at least 24 hours (Shark NV360 guide). A used filter's real performance is unknown and it may hold mould: wash it as the maker says, and don't count on it to clean the air you breathe. It is not a face mask and not a water filter.
- **Belt.** A small belt for a light drive. On the Oreck XL it runs from the motor shaft to the brushroll (iFixit Oreck belt).
- **Brushroll motor.** A small motor in the floor head on some models (iFixit NV360 brush motor). Read its label for voltage before you reuse it.
- **Switches and thermal cut-out.** The NV360 has a three-position switch: off, suction only, and brushroll on (Shark NV360 guide). A salvaged thermal cut-out is not proof of safety: a continuity test shows only that it is closed, never heat one to test it, and don't make it the only protection in anything you build.
- **Hose and wand.** Flexible hose and rigid tube: air ducts for a blower, or a reach tool.
- **Control board.** The NV360 has a small board in the floor head, held by two screws and wired to the brush motor (iFixit NV360 board).

## Variations

- **Belt from the main motor:** the Oreck XL upright drives its brushroll with a belt off the main motor shaft (iFixit Oreck belt).
- **Separate brush motor:** the Shark NV360 has its own roller brush motor and belt in the floor head, and a small board there (iFixit NV360 brush motor, iFixit NV360 board). Its owner's guide gives 120 V, 60 Hz, 1200 W for the whole vacuum (Shark NV360 guide).
- **Bagless with two filters:** the NV360 uses a foam and felt pre-motor kit (XFF350) and a post-motor HEPA (XHF350) (Shark NV360 guide).
- **Canisters with a reel:** the Dyson DC52 reel is held by two Torx T15 screws and a Phillips screw (iFixit DC52 reel).
- Cordless stick vacuums run from lithium packs: see safety_swollen_lithium and teardown_laptop_battery.

## What to leave

- The inside of the cord reel drum. Keep the drum whole.
- Used bags, and torn or clogged filters.
- Cracked hoses and the plastic body, unless you need the plastic.
- A motor with burnt windings or a burnt commutator.
